segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with perfumed oil and wiped his feet with her hair; it was her brother Lazarus who was ill.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the sisters sent word to him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, look, the one you love is ill.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus heard this, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This illness is not to end in death; it is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed for the time being in the place where he was, two days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then, after this, he said to the disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let us go to Judea again.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, just now the Judeans were trying to stone you, and you are going back there?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, they do not stumble, because they see the light of this world.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if anyone walks in the night, they stumble, because the light is not in them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said this, and after that he told them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going to wake him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will get well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus had been speaking about his death, but they thought he was speaking about ordinary sleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then Jesus told them plainly,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Lazarus has died,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let us go too, so that we may die with him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus arrived, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles away,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them about their brother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went to meet him, but Mary remained seated in the house.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Martha said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Your brother will rise.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Martha said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even if they die, will live,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one who is coming into the world.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When she had said this, she went away and called her sister Mary, telling her privately,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Mary heard this, she got up quickly and went to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus had not yet come into the village but was still at the place where Martha had met him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Jews who were with her in the house consoling her, when they saw Mary get up quickly and go out, followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping, he was stirred to anger in spirit and troubled,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Where have you laid him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, come and see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus burst into tears.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Jews said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “See how he loved him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some of them said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man have done something so that this man also would not die?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus, again stirred to anger within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take away the stone.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, by now there is a stench, for it is the fourth day.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Did I not tell you that if you believe you will see the glory of God?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted his eyes upward and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I knew that you always hear me, but I said this for the sake of the crowd standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had said this, he cried out in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Lazarus, come out!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The dead man came out, his feet and hands bound with burial wrappings and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Untie him and let him go.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So many of the Jews, those who had come to Mary and seen what he did, believed in him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some of them went off to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the chief priests and the Pharisees called a meeting of the council and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What are we doing? This man is performing many signs.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You know nothing at all,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: nor do you consider that it is to your advantage that one man should die for the people and the whole nation not perish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not say this on his own, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So from that day on they planned to kill him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus no longer walked about openly among the Jews, but went away from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and he stayed there with the disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up to Jerusalem from the countryside before the Passover to purify themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where he was should report it, so that they could arrest him.

notes.note: Two Greek verbs for love appear in this chapter: one here and in verse 36, another in verse 5. Some interpreters see a distinction between warm affection and a higher love. Most scholars judge that John uses the two interchangeably, and both are rendered 'love' here.

The Greek word covers both 'Jews' and 'Judeans'. Here the contrast is geographic: Jesus is across the Jordan and proposes returning to Judea, where people had tried to stone him. Elsewhere in the chapter the same word is rendered 'Jews'. Scholars are divided: some argue for 'Judeans' throughout, others object that this erases Jews from the New Testament.

The verb is the one usually translated 'save'; used of a sick person it ordinarily means 'recover'. The disciples mean only that sleep is a good sign. A reader of the Greek may well have heard the larger sense too, in keeping with the misunderstandings John often builds into dialogue.

Didymus is the ordinary Greek word for 'twin', and the name Thomas reflects the Aramaic word with the same meaning. John is explaining the name for Greek readers, so it is translated here. Many English versions leave it as 'Didymus'.

Burial normally took place on the day of death. Later rabbinic tradition records a belief that the soul lingered near the body for three days. If that idea was already current, which is uncertain, the fourth day marks the death as beyond all doubt; Martha's remark in verse 39 makes the same point in physical terms.
The Greek says 'about fifteen stadia'. A stadion was roughly 185 metres, so the distance is a little under three kilometres, or somewhat less than two miles.

The Greek word is a title for the anointed king Israel expected, and Martha is confessing that Jesus holds that title. 'Messiah' conveys this to a modern reader, for whom 'Christ' sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep 'Christ' where it works as a name.

notes.traditional: groaned in the spirit / was deeply moved in spirit
notes.note: Elsewhere in the New Testament this verb is used of stern warning or angry rebuke (Mark 1:43; 14:5), and in wider Greek of snorting with anger. Most English versions soften it to 'deeply moved', but many commentators hold that indignation is meant. The text does not say what the anger is directed at: death itself, the grief it causes, or the unbelief of those present have all been proposed. The verb recurs in verse 38.

The verb differs from the one used of Mary and the mourners in verses 31 and 33, which is the usual word for audible lamentation. This one means to shed tears and occurs only here in the New Testament; its tense suggests the onset of the action. 'Jesus wept' is the familiar rendering, but it hides the change of verb.

'Place' most likely means the temple, which Jewish writing of the period often calls 'the place' or 'the holy place'. It could also mean Jerusalem, or the council's own standing. The rendering leaves the Greek as open as it is.

This is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually rendered 'Gentiles'; here, in the singular, it means the Jewish nation as a political body. In verse 50 Caiaphas sets it beside a different word, rendered 'the people', which often refers to Israel as God's people.

The high priesthood was not an annual office, and Caiaphas held it for about eighteen years (roughly AD 18 to 36). Most scholars take John to mean 'in that fateful year', the year of Jesus's death, not that the office changed hands yearly.

candidates.reason: As a form of address (κύριε) it ranges from polite 'sir' to a confession of lordship, and translators split differently verse by verse, especially in the Gospels.
It covers physical recovery, rescue and salvation; a consistent policy is needed for when 'save' is kept and when 'heal/recover' is used, particularly where the author plays on both.
Translations vary between 'council', 'Sanhedrin' and 'a meeting'; readers should see one term for the Jerusalem body across the Gospels and Acts.
Ancient measures recur in the Gospels, Acts and Revelation, and the translation needs one policy on converting to modern units versus keeping the ancient term.
Whether to distinguish φιλέω from ἀγαπάω in English affects several passages in John (notably chapter 21) and should be decided once.
